content.title: Response to Reviewer HpUr
content.comment: We thank the reviewer for the positive evaluation. We agree that it is better to refer Fig. 2 as a stacked neural ODE. In fact, if the neural ODE (1) is not fully connected, then it may become a stacked neural ODE. Therefore, we take the neural ODE in general form as in (1). We will make the architecture of the model clear both in the technical section and experiment settings in the future version of the work. Regarding where the invariance should be backprop to in order to maintain good performance, this is currently under investigation. For now, we just randomly backprop the invariance to a layer as the performance of each layers in deep learning is still not well understood in the literature.

content.title: Response to Reviewer razA
content.comment: We thank the reviewer for the positive evaluation. The proposed method can be applied to complex examples as well, as the barrier functions have been shown to work for humanoids, quadrotors in the literature. We are also working on more complex scenarios like humanoid safe walking, end-to-end vision-based autonomous driving. Preliminary results show good performance of the proposed invariance approach. Note that, the proposed method can be applied to CNNs, such as \dot x = CNN. We are exploring on this in the end-to-end vision-based autonomous driving, and propagate the invariance to images. Since other reviewers complained about the presentation, we are going to withdraw and make sure the technical parts are easier to understand for people who are not familiar with neural ODE and barrier functions.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper developed a principled approach for enforcing specification guarantees on neural ODEs via using invariance set propagation and the barrier function technique. The proposed approach is demonstrated on several representation learning tasks, e.g. spiral curve regression, safe neural control of collision avoidance for autonomous vehicles, etc.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The proposed approach leverages the barrier function in a novel way to enforce forward invariance.

2. The theoretical guarantees are quite strong.

3. The numerical study looks promising.

Weaknesses:
1. It is unclear how scalable the proposed method is. Is it possible to scale the proposed method to more complex examples such as humanoid?

2. As mentioned by the authors, the proposed method cannot be applied to CNNs. This seems to be a strong restriction when considering perception-based control tasks.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes invariance set probation to propagate safety guarantees in the output space of stacked neural ODEs to the input space. They demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on many tasks with a focus on robotics and safe control problems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1) The recursive definition of forward invariance conditions that propagate down the layers allows stacking multiple neural ODEs together. 
2) The experiments show that they can enforce complex barrier conditions by composing 34 constraints together, and filter out noisy Lidar input for safe taking over in autonomous driving. 

Weaknesses:
1) In section 4.1 and Figure 2, instead of referring to the neural ODE architecture as a 3-layer neural ODE, it is more precise to refer to it as a  stacked neural ODE, since there is an integrator after each layer. This needs to be distinguished with the case where a neural ODE that has 3-layer neural networks as the dynamics, but only has one integrator. In addition, I am confused on the architecture setting for the experiments. For instance. in appendix it seems that the architecture used in 6.2 is one neural ODE with 3-layer dynamics (which is different than what suggested in the overview figure Fig 2). Since the optimization in Eq (8) relies on the architecture in Fig.2, I am confused on what QP the authors enforce in 6.2. It'd be helpful if the authors can write the architecture and constraints for each experiment explicitly.

2) When enforcing forward invariance via QP, the authors take out the activation function at layer k, and only makes $\theta_{k,k-1}$ to be decision variable. The benefit of doing so is that the optimization problem in (8) is then a convex optimization problem. However, the potential downside is that the projected $\theta_{k,k-1}$ needs to be very different than the original weight, which will detriment the performance. It'd be good of the authors can provide some discussions on how to decide which layer to backprop the invariance set to, and how that influence the tradeoff between model performance and safety guarantee.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper proposes a novel technique to enforce forward invariance of neural ODEs via invariance set propagation. 
The writing of the paper can be improved:
1) The definition of neural ODE architecture is not clear (See weaknesses 1 for details).
2) In Eq (7), $\psi_{k-2, 1}$ and $\psi_{k-2, 2}$ are not explicitly given (only described in text), it would be helpful if the authors can provide an explicit form (which may involve the jacobians).
3) In the experiment section, it'd be good to mention what methods that are used to enforce invariance. For instance, 6.1-6.3 use projecting the model parameters, and 6.4 projecting the inputs.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes invariance set propagation to achieve specification guarantees in the output space of neural ODEs. The proposed method seems to be correct and effective. However, the writing needs to be more rigorous (architecture, optimization constraints, etc).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work introduces a new approach that ensures a set of specification guarantees for neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs). It is based on what authors call "invariance set propagation", where an invariance of a NODE implies satisfying mathematical formulae, physical laws, and safety. An output constraint (such as positivity) is implemented in the network in a recursive manner (in the backward direction). The procedure involves first training the NODE as usual, and then solving a quadratic program that gives another solution, which (i) is approximately close to the original solution and (ii) satisfies the constraints. The experiments show that the approach respects the constraints without significant performance drop.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- To my knowledge, neural ODEs have never been extended to satisfy (safety) constraints, which is an important problem setup with several real-world applications. In that sense, the paper studies a very interesting problem.
- As far as I understand the methodology, it seems quite general and applicable to many constraints without modifying the original neural ODE training objective. The post-hoc problem "to enforce invariances" also seems constraint/network independent.

Weaknesses:
- The paper is not well-written. First, many consecutive passages don't seem to be related and hence, one needs to put a lot of effort to integrate the ideas. Second, the paper skips many details that are important (to me) whereas certain parts are repetitive. Third, I don't fully understand (parts of) the main theorem and the experiments; therefore, I'm not able to conclude whether the work is sound or not. Please see my "clarity" comments on the next question.
- Experiment details are missing. Please see my comments on the next question.
- Standard ICLR template is modified. If the correct template was used, the paper would surely exceed 9 pages. I'm not sure if this would lead to an automatic rejection but the text must be shortened. I'm hoping that this is not intentional as it would be a very cheap and disrespectful trick.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Novelty:** As far as I know, NODEs have never been equipped with safety constraints. Furthermore, although High Order Control Barrier Function (HOCBF) theory was already proposed, this paper shows how it can be applied to more complex neural net-based models.

**Quality:** Despite the nice ideas and novel construction, the paper suffers from significant presentation issues. Most of them are noted below but here are additional more generic ones:
- The figures are very difficult to follow as a lot of information is squeezed into very small areas.
- Motivation is missing:
  - The paper starts with the methodology itself. The problem is not clearly defined and the motivation is missing. As such, one would have difficulty understanding if/why this is an important problem after all.
  - *The key idea is to do invariance propagation for neural ODEs using High Order Control Barrier Function (HOCBF) theory*. Why this method instead of others? This should also be motivated. Also, HOCBF should be briefly explained/discussed before listing the limitations.
- Notation and terminology should be fixed. Please see my comments below.
- Discussion is completely missing.

**Clarity:** I believe the entire text should be revised. Here are some tips:
- In my understanding, the method is defined for neural networks in general, not just neural ODEs. Similarly, sentences like "*Thus, we can denote the relative degree of a neuron in a neural ODE by...*" reads wrong ("a neuron in NODE" should be replaced with "a neuron in NN differential function approximation"). Another example is *the three-layer neural ODE*.
- The paper lacks an important discussion on why their approach is called "invariant". I'm not sure if it is related to the concept of "remaining the same after transformations".
- *To this end, we explore control-theoretic invariance*. This should be elaborated as the reader might be unfamiliar with the concept.
- *explicit and implicit data patterns* should be explained too.
- The first paragraph is very long and it delivers multiple ideas; should be split into 2+ paragraphs. 
- *we address the possible conservativeness of the invariance by including invariance functions in the training loop*. "possible conservativeness of the invariance" should be explained/exemplified.
- Related work lists the previous methods involving neural ODEs, set invariances, and filters whereas these concepts are not properly explained/discussed.
- Explaining OptNet before discussing the issues with it being not trainable would help the reader understand the issues better. Also, it should be explained why it is not trainable despite being differentiable. 
- *verification-in-the-loop training* and what is meant by *coverage of the entire state space* should be explained.
- *This optimization problem can then be solved and trained end-to-end by reverse mode automatic differentiation*. This is grammatically wrong since  the optimization problem is not trained.
- Does the model only handle inequality constraints? If so, this should be clearly stated.
- In Sec4.1, "relative degree" should be defined before going into the details. 
- *connection relationship between neurons*. Should be revised for clarity.
- *In order to formulate a differentiable QP*. It is not clear why we need a differential QP after all.
- *we only drop the activation functions of layer $k − 1$*. Wouldn't this cause a problem as the activations would suddently change (and hence the network output)?
- *make the differentiable QP not conservative*. What is a "conservative QP"?
- *has shown to work in* is very informal. The context should be made clear.
- Does Sec5 differ from the discussion so far? It seems mostly identical and repetitive to me.
- *The focus is on the specification guarantees rather than accuracy of models.* Then what is the point of numerical comparisons?


Experiment details should be included. 
  - What are the optimization objectives? 
  - Is the NODE defined in a latent space as in the original paper (Chen 18)?
  - *This can be done after the training using the proposed invariance or during the training.* How to do these should be clearly explained.
  - What are the "34 safety constraints" in Sec6.2?
  - How is the experiment in Sec6.3 performed? How exactly is a sequential model (NODE) used to fit three parameters? How come *x,y are functions of t$?


Notation/terminology-related comments:
- $\dot{x}(t)$ should be defined. Also, time derivatives and Jacobians should be distinguished.
- *$x \in R^n$ is the neuron state* is wrong. It is the state of the system.
- *the output of the neural ODE is the integration solution of (1)*. The integral should be explicitly given.
- *Input observations $I(t)$* should be defined, in particular, how it differs from $x^\text{obs}$.
- *There is an odeint after each layer* is vague, should be stated properly.
- *We denote the neuron vectors as $x_r$ in which the relative degrees of all neuron components are $r − 1$*. What does "neuron vector" mean?
- *Then $x = (x_1 , . . . , x_{m+1})$, where*. What is $x$ here? The state vector $x(t)$ or one layer in the neural net?
- *first-from-the-last hidden layer invariance* is not clear.
- $\psi_m(...)$ takes the whole vector $x$ as input in Theorem1 unlike other places in the text, e.g., eq5.
- The beginning of the Proof starts as $b(x)>0$ and ends with *when $b(x)=0$*. This looks wrong.
- Concerning secong proof; I either suggest skipping it or including more details since current proof (*The proof is identical to that of Theorem 1.*) is not scientific at all.
- *In the second stage, we train the differentiable QP (specifically, the parameter $p_{k−1}$ in QP (8))* contradicts with eq8, which defines the optimization problem for $\theta_{k,k−1}$.
- *$u = x_1$ is its control (i.e., the output of the neural ODE).* Does that imply another differential equation system (in addition to eq14)?

Minor comments:
- neural Ordinary **Differential** Equations
- *The satisfaction of the corresponding constraints implies the satisfaction of output specifications.* is repetitive.
- In this work, **we** address
- *Our proposed invariance back-propagates the output specification all the way to the input layer (or model parameters)* is repeated many times.
- Multiple citations should be given inside a single pair of parentheses: (Kim et al., 2021, Alvarez et al., 2020, Baker et al., 2022) instead of (Kim et al., 2021) (Alvarez et al., 2020) (Baker et al., 2022).
- *The differentiable optimizations are usually served as a layer (filter) in the neural networks*. This sentence is grammatically wrong. Also To my knowledge, "differentiable optimization layers" is more commonly used than "filters".
- *... temporal dynamics with neural agents deployed in control settings*. What does neural agent mean here?
- *This is shown in the invariance enforcing section*. This particular point should be referred.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper proposes a novel approach to enable NODEs to satisfy inequality constraints. As shown by the autonomous driving experiment in Sec 6.4, the approach comes with important real-world applications. Yet the paper should be rejected since (i) the notation and terminology are problematic, (ii) many passages in the text are not clear at all, and (iii) important experiment details are missing. As such, the manuscript would create significant confusion in the community.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper deals with the problem of imposing constraints on the solution of a Neural ODE.

Given an output specification that imposes some property over the output of a Neural ODE (this takes the form of specification function that should remain positive), a strategy based on a method called HOCBF theory is proposed to convert this specification over the output into a set of constraint over the other components of the state of the ODE recursively (such that if those intermediate constraints are satisfied, the output constraint will be satisfied).

The strategy is then to impose, through the use of the differentiable optimization layer (which allows the imposition of constraints), that the intermediate constraints get satisfied. Because the intermediate constraints get satisfied, this means that the output constraint will also be satisfied.

In term of the full training strategy proposed, the training is done in two parts. A first training is done to learn the Neural ODE without taking into account the constraints. Then, the optimization problem of imposing the constraints is solved, while trying to minimize the difference with the original parameters.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength
The problem setting is quite interesting, and being able to ensure that certain properties will be respected when using a control policy is very valuable. The empirical evaluation is performed over different settings. 

# Weaknesses

## Clarity of the paper
I think that the paper's clarity is its main probelm, as the paper is hard to parse. Variables and notations are used without being rigorously defined, leaving the reader to guess the intended meaning, making it quite hard to follow.
- In Equation (2), what do observed state and predicted state means? Is it assumed that the task is a regression state where $x^{obs}(t)$ is given, and $x^{pre}(t)$ corresponds to evaluating the Neural ODE? Should equation (2) be summed/integrated over t, or is the loss only defined at the last t? More generally, the goal of the paper is not actually clearly defined anywhere. From what I gather, the objective is to solve the minimization problem of Equation (2), subject to the dynamics given by equation (3), while imposing some constraints $h(x(t)) \geq 0 \quad \forall t$. This should be explained somewhere!
- The notion of "neuron" of an ODE used in Section 4 is not clearly defined. Does it correspond to one coordinate of the state x? Or does it correspond to an activation of the neural network $NN_\theta$?
- In equation 4, why are the dependency of $\dot{h}$ on $x_2$ and $\theta_{2, 1}$ made explicit? Also, it's unclear with regards to what is $\dot{h}$ a derivative? Is it with respect to the time $t$?
- For theorem 1, I assume that it means that the condition $\psi_m(x, \theta) \geq 0$ needs to hold for all $t$?
- In subsection 4.3, what does it mean to "drop the activation functions" of a layer? Does it mean that the architecture of the Neural ODE get modified, so that the problem of imposing the constraints becomes tractable, and so the final Neural ODE will have a different architecture? 
- Certain terms are not defined. What does the measure of "deadlock rate" correspond to? Where is it shown that "intersampling" is solved for the proposed method, as claimed by Section 6.1? 
- Why is the method called "Forward invariance"? The word "forward" appears only in the naming of the method (in the title and in the related works), while it seems to me that the invariants are actually propagated backward, from the state back to the intermediate neuron.
- How are the $alpha$ function chosen? The papers says that they need to be carefully chosen (Section 6.1) but nowhere does it explain how? What form do they take?
- Missing from the paper is also an overview describing how the proposed method is actually happening, under the form of an algorithm. What are the inputs to the procedure, what are the different steps that are taken in order to reach the output (the parameters $\theta$), and how can you show that these parameters have the desired properties. Figure 3 is absolutely not informative, as it does not reflect how the invariant are specified, does not indicate how the ODE is trained.

## Novelty
The construction of $\psi_m(x, \theta)$ seems to be similar to Equation (10) to (12) of (Xiao & Belta, 2022), with the proof of Theorem 1 being the same as the one of Theorem 3 of that paper. More generally, I found it extremely hard to distinguish what in the paper represented contribution of the authors vs. what was a result of the Xiao & Belta paper. I would recommend the author to restructure the paper significantly, by first introducing the main results of HOCBF theory for classical ODEs and how they are used to enforce safety constraints. Given this, they should highlight what part transfer to the Neural ODE setting, and what part do not. It would then be possible to introduce their solution in a contextualized manner. 

## Questions:
- In the related work section, the authors make the claim that "OptNet is not trainable", even though making optimization layers differentiable (and therefore trainable) was the whole point of the OptNet paper? Could the authors clarify what they mean?
- The authors claim that one of the limitations of the HOCBF method is that it can only be applied to affine control systems. This is said in the introduction, as well as at the end of section 5. On the other hand, it seems that given the simplification made in equation (6), this is also the requirements of the method proposed. Could the authors clarify what are the differences?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity of the work is the main problem, as discussed above, and it makes it fairly difficult to assess the correctness of the work. 
The originality is also hard to assess because the work is not properly presented in context and does not really delineate where existing results ends and where theirs start.
In terms of reproducibility, the authors attached their code as a supplementary material, but it would be extremely hard to reproduce the results without it as all explanations are very imprecise.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper was hard to review. It seems to present interesting empirical results that showcase the ability to enforce the respect of some constraints over the trajectories generated by the neural ODEs, but the presentation of the method is too imprecise to accurately judge it.
I think that this paper might have a lot of potential but is unsuitable for publication at this moment.

content.title: On the Forward Invariance of Neural ODEs
content.TL;DR: This paper proposes to achieve specification guarantees in the output space of neural ODEs with invariance set propagation.
content.abstract: To ensure robust and trustworthy decision-making, it is highly desirable to enforce constraints over a neural network's parameters and its inputs automatically by back-propagating output specifications. This way, we can guarantee that the network makes reliable decisions under perturbations. Here, we propose a new method for achieving a class of specification guarantees for neural Ordinary Differentiable Equations (ODEs) by using invariance set propagation. An invariance of a neural ODE is defined as an output specification, such as to satisfy mathematical formulae, physical laws, and system safety. We use control barrier functions to specify the invariance of a neural ODE on the output layer and propagate it back to the input layer. Through the invariance backpropagation, we map output specifications onto constraints on the neural ODE parameters or its input. The satisfaction of the corresponding constraints implies the satisfaction of output specifications. This allows us to achieve output specification guarantees by changing the input or parameters while maximally preserving the model performance. We demonstrate the invariance propagation on a comprehensive series of representation learning tasks, including spiral curve regression, autoregressive modeling of joint physical dynamics, convexity portrait of a function, and safe neural control of collision avoidance for autonomous vehicles.
